title: Physics Foundations: Set 1
description: Twelve original questions on motion, forces, energy, thermal transfers and waves. Independently authored by Neumeris.

questions.prompt: The graph shows the displacement x of a camera carriage along a straight rail. Determine its speed between t = 0 and t = 4.0 s. [1]
questions.hint: Read the displacement at each end of the 0–4.0 s segment. Calculate (final displacement − initial displacement)/(elapsed time), then take the magnitude to obtain speed.
notes: On a displacement–time graph, velocity is the gradient Δx/Δt. Use the change between two positions, rather than a position measured from the origin; this works even when the initial displacement is non-zero.
Speed is the magnitude of velocity. A downward-sloping segment gives negative velocity but positive speed; a horizontal segment gives zero velocity because the position does not change.

diagram.alt: Displacement–time graph joining (0 s, 14 m), (4 s, 4 m) and (6 s, 4 m).

answer.explanation: Velocity = (4 − 14)/(4 − 0) = −2.5 m s⁻¹. Speed is the magnitude of velocity, 2.5 m s⁻¹. B divides the initial position by time; C gives signed velocity; D uses displacement change without dividing by time.

questions.prompt: An inspection robot moves along a straight tunnel. Its velocity v is positive towards the tunnel entrance. The graph shows its motion for 6.0 s.
questions.hint: Treat the areas under the velocity–time graph differently for displacement and distance.

part_hints.label: a
part_hints.hint: Split the graph into rectangles and triangles at its corners and at the zero-velocity crossing. Add their areas with a negative sign for regions below the time axis.

part_hints.label: b
part_hints.hint: Use the same rectangles and triangles as in part (a), but add every area as a positive magnitude because travel in either direction contributes to distance.

part_hints.label: c
part_hints.hint: Think about what happens to velocity direction when the graph crosses the time axis.

notes: Displacement is the signed area under a velocity–time graph. Opposite-direction sections can cancel, so zero displacement means the final position equals the initial position, even if substantial motion occurred.

Distance is the area under the speed–time graph, equivalently the sum of the magnitudes of velocity–time areas. When velocity changes sign within a straight segment, split that segment at the zero crossing before finding the areas.

diagram.alt: Velocity–time graph joining (0 s, 3 m s⁻¹), (2 s, 3 m s⁻¹), (4 s, −3 m s⁻¹) and (6 s, −3 m s⁻¹).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the displacement of the robot during the 6.0 s. [2]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total distance travelled during the 6.0 s. [2]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the answers to (a) and (b) differ. [2]

answer.explanation: Worked answers and one-mark criteria are given for each part.

marking_points.text: Uses signed areas under the velocity–time graph, with negative area below the axis.
Obtains 0 m from 6 + 1.5 − 1.5 − 6.
Adds the magnitudes of the positive and negative areas, including the two reversal triangles.
Obtains 15 m.

parts.label: c
parts.answer: The robot reverses direction; opposite signed displacements cancel, but all motion contributes positively to distance.
parts.working: The velocity changes sign, so the robot travels in opposite directions. Signed areas cancel in displacement; absolute areas add in distance.

marking_points.text: Identifies reversal of direction when velocity changes sign.
Explains signed cancellation for displacement versus addition of magnitudes for distance.

questions.prompt: A small ring is in translational equilibrium under three forces in a horizontal plane. Two forces acting on the ring are shown. Determine the magnitude and direction of the third force. [1]
questions.hint: Find the horizontal and vertical components of the resultant of the two shown forces. For equilibrium the third force must cancel both components; use Pythagoras for its magnitude.
notes: Translational equilibrium requires the vector sum of all forces to be zero. To find a missing force, reverse the components of the resultant of the known forces; matching only its magnitude is insufficient.

For perpendicular components Fx and Fy, the resultant magnitude is √(Fx² + Fy²). Use vector geometry rather than adding or subtracting force magnitudes, and use the component signs to identify the direction.

diagram.alt: Top view of a ring with a 6.0 N force to the right and an 8.0 N force upwards on the page. Only two of the three forces are shown.

answer.explanation: The resultant of the shown forces has magnitude √(6.0² + 8.0²) = 10 N and points upwards and rightwards. The third force is its opposite: components 6.0 N leftwards and 8.0 N downwards. A adds magnitudes; B has the wrong direction; C subtracts magnitudes.

questions.prompt: A 0.40 kg ball travels horizontally towards a vertical cushion at 5.0 m s⁻¹ and rebounds at 3.0 m s⁻¹ along the same line. The contact time is 0.080 s. Take the direction towards the cushion as positive. Consider only the horizontal motion.
questions.hint: Keep the stated positive direction when using momentum change and contact time.

part_hints.label: a
part_hints.hint: Write the initial and rebound velocities with signs using the direction towards the cushion as positive. Substitute them into J = m(v − u).

part_hints.label: b
part_hints.hint: Divide the signed impulse from (a) by the contact time.

part_hints.label: c
part_hints.hint: Compare the force on the ball with the force on the cushion in the same contact. Use the ball’s force direction to infer the cushion’s.

notes: Impulse equals the change in momentum, J = m(v − u), for constant mass. In a rebound the velocities have opposite signs, so the magnitude of the velocity change is the sum of the incoming and outgoing speeds.

Average resultant force equals impulse divided by interaction time. For the same momentum change, a longer contact time reduces the average force magnitude; the impulse and average force have the same direction.
Forces two bodies exert on each other in the same interaction have equal magnitudes and opposite directions, even when their accelerations differ.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the horizontal impulse on the ball. [2]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average horizontal resultant force on the ball during contact. [1]

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the average horizontal force exerted by the ball on the cushion and explain its direction. [2]

answer.explanation: Worked answers and one-mark criteria are given for each part.

marking_points.text: Uses J = m(v − u) with a negative rebound velocity.
Obtains −3.2 N s, or 3.2 N s away from the cushion.
Obtains −40 N, or 40 N away from the cushion, with consistent follow-through from (a).

parts.label: c
parts.working: The cushion exerts −40 N on the ball. The ball exerts +40 N on the cushion by Newton’s third law.

marking_points.text: States equal magnitude 40 N towards the cushion (positive direction).
Explains the forces are an equal-and-opposite Newton third-law pair acting on different bodies.

questions.prompt: A cable exerts a constant force of 30 N on a crate. The cable is at 60° to the horizontal. The crate moves 4.0 m horizontally to the right. Calculate the work done by the cable force. [1]
questions.hint: Resolve the cable force along the horizontal displacement. Multiply that component, F cos θ with θ measured from the horizontal here, by the distance moved.
notes: Work by a constant force is W = Fs cos θ, where θ is the angle between that force and displacement. Re-identify this angle if the diagram or direction of motion changes; the relevant component is always the one parallel to displacement.

A force component perpendicular to displacement does no work. The sign of work depends on the parallel component: it is positive along the motion and negative against it, so work done by one force is distinct from net work by all forces.

diagram.alt: Crate pulled upwards and rightwards by a cable at 60 degrees to the horizontal; displacement is horizontal to the right.

answer.explanation: W = Fs cos θ = 30 × 4.0 × cos 60° = 60 J. A omits the projection, C uses sin 60°, and D divides by cos 60° instead of multiplying.

questions.prompt: During an 8.0 s lift, a motor receives 5.0 kJ of electrical energy. The useful increase in gravitational potential energy of the load is 3.2 kJ.
questions.hint: Identify the useful output energy before choosing an energy ratio or a power calculation.

part_hints.label: a
part_hints.hint: Form useful energy/input energy using the two energies for this lift. Use matching units, then multiply the ratio by 100 if giving a percentage.

part_hints.label: b
part_hints.hint: Use the load’s useful energy gain, rather than the motor’s input energy. Convert that gain to joules and divide by the lift time to obtain watts.

part_hints.label: c
part_hints.hint: Subtract useful energy from electrical input, then name a plausible energy store of the motor or surroundings.

notes: Efficiency is useful output energy divided by input energy for the same process. Matching energy units cancel in the ratio; increasing wasted energy while holding input energy fixed lowers efficiency.

Average useful output power is useful energy transferred divided by elapsed time. Use joules and seconds for watts, and distinguish useful output power from input power by choosing the appropriate energy; for the same interval their ratio is the efficiency.
Input energy is accounted for as useful output plus transfers to other stores, often thermal energy from friction or electrical resistance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the efficiency of the motor for this lift. [2]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average useful output power. [1]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the energy not transferred usefully and suggest where it goes. [2]

answer.explanation: Worked answers and one-mark criteria are given for each part.

marking_points.text: Uses useful energy divided by input energy.
Obtains 0.64 or 64%.
Obtains 400 W using 3200 J divided by 8.0 s.

parts.label: c
parts.answer: 1.8 kJ; mainly thermal energy in the motor and surroundings
parts.working: 5.0 − 3.2 = 1.8 kJ. Resistive heating and friction transfer this energy to thermal stores (and possibly sound).

marking_points.text: Obtains 1.8 kJ of non-usefully transferred energy.
Identifies a plausible dissipative transfer, such as resistive heating or frictional heating.

questions.prompt: A 0.25 kg aluminium block is heated from 20°C to 60°C. Its specific heat capacity is 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. No change of state occurs. Calculate the increase in its internal energy. [1]
questions.hint: Subtract the initial temperature from the final temperature, then use ΔU = mcΔT with the given mass and specific heat capacity. A Celsius temperature difference has the same numerical value in kelvin.
notes: For heating without a change of state, the energy increase is mcΔT. Use the temperature rise rather than the final temperature; for fixed material properties the energy scales with both mass and temperature rise.

Temperature differences have the same numerical value in kelvin and degrees Celsius. Add 273 only when converting an absolute Celsius temperature to kelvin; if a change of state occurs, include the appropriate latent energy separately.

answer.explanation: ΔU = mcΔT = 0.25 × 900 × (60 − 20) = 9000 J. A omits ΔT, B omits mass, and D uses 60°C as the temperature change.

questions.prompt: A 0.20 kg metal sample at 70°C is placed in 0.15 kg of water at 20°C. The specific heat capacities of the metal and water are 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ respectively. The container is thermally insulated and has negligible heat capacity. Neither substance changes state. They reach a common final temperature.
questions.hint: Use conservation of energy and each substance’s total heat capacity.

part_hints.label: a
part_hints.hint: Call the common final temperature T. Write the metal’s lost energy as mmetal cmetal(70 − T) and the water’s gained energy as mwater cwater(T − 20), set them equal and solve for T.

part_hints.label: b
part_hints.hint: Calculate mc for each substance, then use ΔT = Q/(mc). Explain which substance changes temperature less when both exchange the same amount of energy.

notes: For an insulated two-body system with negligible container heat capacity and no phase change, energy lost by the hotter body equals energy gained by the colder body. Use one common final temperature and positive temperature-change magnitudes; the result should lie between the initial temperatures.

Total heat capacity is mc, so both mass and material matter. In this setup the final temperature is a heat-capacity-weighted mean of the initial temperatures and lies closer to that of the body with larger mc, since equal transferred energy changes its temperature less.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the final temperature is closer to the water’s initial temperature than to the metal’s initial temperature. [1]

answer.explanation: The worked answers and marking points are given for each part.

marking_points.text: Sets heat lost by metal equal to heat gained by water with correct masses and temperature differences.
Solves to obtain 31°C; accept 31.1°C.

parts.label: b
parts.answer: The water has the larger total heat capacity, so the same transferred energy causes a smaller temperature change in the water.
parts.working: mc for water = 630 J K⁻¹; mc for metal = 180 J K⁻¹. Equal energy transfer therefore produces a smaller change in water temperature.

marking_points.text: Relates the water’s larger mc to its smaller temperature change for the same energy transfer.

questions.prompt: A light ray is incident on a plane boundary at 40° to the normal. The speed of light is 2.4 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in medium X and 1.6 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in medium Y. The ray is transmitted from X into Y. Which range contains the angle r between the transmitted ray and the normal? [1]
questions.hint: Substitute the speeds into sin r = (vY/vX) sin i. Compare the resulting sine with sin 40°, then use the fact that sine increases between 0° and 90° to select the angle range.
notes: Snell’s law can be written sin r/sin i = v2/v1, with both angles measured from the normal. Entering a slower medium makes a transmitted ray bend towards the normal; entering a faster medium makes it bend away, when transmission is possible.

Total internal reflection is possible only for travel towards a faster medium and incidence above the critical angle. Check both the speed ordering and the incident angle in a changed problem; a transition towards a slower medium cannot meet that condition.

diagram.alt: Ray in medium X incident at 40 degrees to a dashed normal at a flat boundary with medium Y. The transmitted ray is not drawn.

answer.explanation: sin r = (1.6/2.4) sin 40° < sin 40°. Since refraction angles here lie between 0° and 90°, r is less than 40° and the ray bends towards the normal (r is about 25°). The non-zero incidence excludes r = 0°.

questions.prompt: Two coherent wave sources oscillate in phase and produce waves of wavelength 0.60 m in the same medium. Their distances from point P are 2.4 m and 3.3 m. Each wave has displacement amplitude 4.0 mm at P. Reflections can be neglected.
questions.hint: Relate the difference in travel distances to phase, then apply superposition.

part_hints.label: a
part_hints.hint: Subtract the shorter source-to-P distance from the longer one to find the path difference.

part_hints.label: b
part_hints.hint: Divide the path difference from part (a) by the wavelength. For sources initially in phase, decide the arrival phase relation, then use the stated equal amplitudes to explain the resultant displacement.

part_hints.label: c
part_hints.hint: Divide Q’s path difference by the wavelength. Decide whether it is a whole number or a half-integer number of wavelengths and apply the interference condition for in-phase sources.

notes: For coherent sources initially in phase, path differences nλ give arrivals in phase and constructive interference, while (n + ½)λ gives antiphase arrivals and destructive interference. Recalculate Δd/λ if distances or wavelength change; an initial source phase difference must also be included if the sources are not in phase.

Superposition adds instantaneous displacements. Antiphase waves cancel completely only when their amplitudes at the observation point are equal; with unequal amplitudes their minimum resultant amplitude is the magnitude of the amplitude difference.

Use the difference between source-to-point distances as the path difference, rather than their sum. A whole-wavelength change in this difference preserves the arrival phase relation, while a half-wavelength change switches between in-phase and antiphase arrivals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the path difference at P. [1]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the resultant displacement amplitude at P is zero. [2]

parts.label: c
parts.text: At another point Q, the path difference is 1.2 m. State the type of interference at Q. [1]

answer.explanation: The worked answers and marking points are given for each part.

marking_points.text: Obtains 0.90 m.

parts.label: b
parts.answer: The path difference is 1.5 wavelengths, so the waves arrive in antiphase. Their equal amplitudes cancel by superposition.
parts.working: 0.90/0.60 = 1.5. This is a half-integer number of wavelengths, so one wave is half a cycle out of phase with the other. The resultant amplitude is |4.0 − 4.0| = 0 mm.

marking_points.text: Identifies the half-integer wavelength path difference as producing antiphase/destructive interference.
Uses equal amplitudes and superposition to explain complete cancellation.

parts.label: c
parts.working: 1.2/0.60 = 2, a whole number of wavelengths, so the waves arrive in phase.

marking_points.text: States constructive interference.

questions.prompt: A fixed-frequency sound source produces two successive resonances in tube A when its air-column lengths are 0.22 m and 0.66 m. Tube A has one open end and one end closed by a movable piston. The same source is then used with tube B, which is open at both ends. The speed of sound is the same in both tubes. Neglect end corrections. Determine the shortest length of tube B that resonates with the source. [1]
questions.hint: Use the difference between tube A’s successive resonance lengths as λ/2 to find the wavelength. Then sketch the shortest displacement standing wave with antinodes at both open ends of tube B.
notes: For a closed–open air column, a closed end is a displacement node and an open end is a displacement antinode. Allowed lengths are odd quarter-wavelengths, so successive resonance lengths differ by λ/2; the spacing can determine wavelength without assuming the first observed resonance is the first harmonic.

An open–open column has displacement antinodes at both ends and its shortest resonant length is λ/2. Transfer the wavelength between tubes only when frequency and wave speed stay the same, then apply the new end conditions rather than reusing the first tube’s first observed resonant length.

diagram.alt: Two separate tube setups: tube A is open on the left and closed by a movable piston on the right, with air-column length Lₐ; tube B is open at both ends, with length Lᵦ. No standing-wave patterns are drawn.

answer.explanation: For tube A, λ/2 = 0.66 − 0.22 = 0.44 m, so λ = 0.88 m. The shortest resonant length for tube B, open at both ends, is λ/2 = 0.44 m. A uses the closed–open first-harmonic length, C uses a whole wavelength, and D uses three half-wavelengths rather than the shortest open–open mode.

questions.prompt: A small platform is suspended from a spring. Its natural frequency is 3.0 Hz. A motor applies a periodic force of constant amplitude while its driving frequency is varied slowly. The platform is initially lightly damped, and its steady-state oscillation amplitude is measured at each driving frequency.
questions.hint: Use the relationship between driving and natural frequencies, then consider the energy balance as damping changes.

part_hints.label: a
part_hints.hint: Compare the forcing rhythm with the platform’s own oscillation rhythm. Then reason about energy transferred in each cycle and how a steady amplitude is reached.

part_hints.label: b
part_hints.hint: Relate stronger damping to energy lost each cycle and to how selectively the platform responds across different driving frequencies.

notes: Resonance occurs when driving is near a system’s natural frequency, allowing effective repeated energy transfer. The driving frequency is imposed externally, while the natural frequency belongs to the free system; if mass or stiffness changes, compare the driver with the new natural frequency. For a lightly damped system the displacement-amplitude maximum is close to, but need not equal, the undamped natural frequency.

At steady state the energy supplied over a cycle balances the energy dissipated. With the same driving-force amplitude, increased damping lowers the maximum displacement amplitude and broadens a distinct resonance peak, making the response less selective in frequency; this peak description assumes the damping remains low enough for a distinct peak.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the platform reaches a large but finite steady-state amplitude near 3.0 Hz. [3]

parts.label: b
parts.text: The damping is increased while the driving-force amplitude is unchanged. The platform remains lightly damped with a distinct resonance peak. State the changes to the maximum amplitude and the width of the peak in the amplitude–driving-frequency response curve. [2]

answer.explanation: Worked answers and one-mark criteria are given for each part.

parts.label: a
parts.answer: Near the natural frequency, resonance transfers energy efficiently; amplitude grows until energy supplied per cycle equals energy dissipated by damping.
parts.working: At driving frequency near 3.0 Hz, resonance produces repeated favourable energy input. The amplitude grows; the steady state is reached when energy input per cycle balances damped losses.

marking_points.text: Identifies resonance when driving frequency is near the natural frequency.
Explains efficient repeated energy transfer from the driver to the platform.
Explains finite steady-state amplitude by energy input balancing damping losses.

parts.label: b
parts.answer: The maximum amplitude decreases and the resonance peak becomes broader.
parts.working: The larger dissipation reduces the maximum steady-state amplitude. With a distinct resonance still present, the response is less selective in frequency, so the peak is broader.

marking_points.text: States that the maximum amplitude decreases.
States that the resonance peak broadens (the response becomes less sharply peaked).
